source_text: Sed aliam argumentationem, eorum convenimus, exigentes cur animalem carnem subeundo Christus animam carnalem videatur habuisse. Deus enim, inquiunt, gestivit animam visibilem hominibus exhibere, faciendo eam corpus, quae retro invisibilis extiterit, natura nihil, nec semetipsam, videns prae impedimento carnis huius, ut etiam disceptaretur nata anima an non. Itaque animam corpus effectam in Christo, ut eam et nascentem et morientem, et quod sit amplius, resurgentem videremus. Et hoc autem quale erat ut per carnem demonstraretur anima sibi aut nobis, quae per carnem non poterat agnosci, ut sic ostenderetur, dum id fit cui latebat, id est caro? Tenebras videlicet accepit ut lucere posset. Denique ad hoc prius retractemus an isto modo ostendenda fuerit anima, dehinc an in totum invisibilem eam retro allegent, utrum quasi incorporalem, an etiam habentem aliquod genus corporis proprii. Et tamen cum invisibilem dicant, corporalem eam constituunt, habentem quod invisibile sit. Nihil enim habens invisibile quomodo potest invisibilis dici? Sed ne esse quidem potest nisi habens per quod sit. Cum autem sit, habeat necesse est aliquid per quod est. Si habet aliquid per quod est, hoc erit corpus eius. Omne quod est, corpus est sui generis. Nihil est incorporale nisi quod non est. Habente igitur anima invisibile corpus, qui visibilem eam facere susceperat utique dignius id eius visibile fecisset quod invisibile habebatur, quia nec hic mendacium aut infirmitas deo competit; mendacium, si aliud animam quam quod erat demonstravit, infirmitas, si id quod erat demonstrare non valuit. Nemo ostendere volens hominem cassidem aut personam ei inducit. Hoc autem factum est animae, si in carne conversa alienam induit superficiem. Sed et si incorporalis anima deputetur, ut aliqua vi rationis occulta sit quidem anima, corpus tamen non sit, quicquid est anima, proinde impossibile deo non erat, et proposito eius congruentius competebat, nova aliqua corporis specie eam demonstrare quam ista communi omnium, alterius iam notitiae, ne sine causa visibilem ex invisibili facere gestisset animam, istis scilicet quaestionibus opportunam, per carnis in illam humanae defensionem. Sed non poterat Christus inter homines nisi homo videri. Redde igitur Christo fidem suam, ut qui homo voluerit incedere, animam quoque humanae condicionis ostenderit, non faciens eam carneam, sed induens eam carne.
thought_title: Refuting the claim that Christ's soul was made visible by becoming flesh
orientation: Tertullian is answering the view of Apelles and his followers that Christ took a soul-made body so that the previously invisible soul could be seen.
pass_a_gloss: But we meet another argument of theirs, demanding why Christ, by undergoing flesh made of soul, seems to have had a fleshly soul. For God, they say, desired to show a visible soul to human beings, by making it a body, which previously had been invisible, seeing nothing by nature, not even itself, because of the hindrance of this flesh, so that it was even debated whether the soul was born or not. And so the soul was made a body in Christ, so that we might see it being born and dying, and what is more, rising again. But what kind of thing was this, that the soul should be shown through flesh to itself or to us, which through flesh could not be recognized, so that it should be shown in this way, while that becomes the thing in which it lay hidden, that is, flesh? It received darkness, of course, so that it could shine. Finally, for this purpose let us first reconsider whether the soul ought to have been shown in this way, then whether they claim that it was wholly invisible before, whether as if incorporeal, or also as having some kind of body of its own. And yet when they say it is invisible, they make it corporeal, having that which is invisible. For having nothing invisible, how can it be called invisible? But it cannot even exist unless it has that through which it exists. But when it exists, it must have something through which it exists. If it has something through which it exists, this will be its body. Everything that exists is a body of its own kind. Nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist. Therefore since the soul has an invisible body, he who had undertaken to make it visible would certainly have more worthily made that visible which was held to be invisible, because neither falsehood nor weakness befits God; falsehood, if he showed the soul as other than it was, weakness, if he was not able to show what it was. No one wishing to show a man puts a helmet or a mask on him. But this was done to the soul, if converted into flesh it put on a foreign surface. But even if the soul is considered incorporeal, so that by some force of reason the soul is indeed hidden, yet is not a body, whatever the soul is, therefore it was not impossible for God, and it was more fittingly suited to his purpose, to show it by some new kind of body than by this common one of all, of another's already known nature, lest he had desired without cause to make the soul visible from invisible, exposed of course to these questions, through the defense of human flesh against it. But Christ could not be seen among human beings except as a man. Give back therefore to Christ his own trustworthiness, so that he who willed to walk as a man also showed a soul of human condition, not making it fleshly, but clothing it with flesh.

choices.why: The glossary bans 'animal' and 'soulish'; 'made of soul' preserves the heretical claim that the flesh was soul-substance.
Keeps the parallel with 'flesh made of soul' and the glossary's 'flesh' for caro; 'carnal' is avoided as a banned sense.

choices.english: is a body of its own kind
choices.why: Renders the philosophical claim literally; 'sui generis' is kept as a recognizable Latinism but glossed in English.
rejected: is a body of its own genus
is a body in its own right

choices.why: Both nouns are concrete and literal; 'mask' for persona avoids the later theological sense of 'person'.
Literal rendering of the clothing metaphor; 'surface' keeps the sense of an outer covering distinct from the soul's own body.

choices.english: Give back therefore to Christ his own trustworthiness
choices.why: Fides here means faithfulness or trustworthiness, not 'faith' in the credal sense; the possessive 'suam' is kept.

pass_b_english: But let us meet them on another argument, demanding why Christ, by taking on flesh made of soul, should be thought to have had a fleshly soul. For God, they say, eagerly desired to display a visible soul to human beings by making it a body—a soul that had previously been invisible, seeing nothing by nature, not even itself, because of the hindrance of this flesh, so that it was even debated whether the soul had been born or not. And so the soul was made a body in Christ, so that we might see it being born, dying, and—what is more—rising again. But what sort of thing was this, that the soul should be demonstrated through flesh to itself or to us, when it could not be recognized through flesh, and so it was shown by becoming the very thing in which it lay hidden—that is, flesh? It took on darkness, apparently, so that it could shine. Let us first reconsider, then, whether the soul ought to have been displayed in this way, and then whether they claim it was entirely invisible before—whether as incorporeal, or as having some kind of body of its own. And yet when they call it invisible, they make it corporeal, since it has something that is invisible. For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible? But it cannot even exist unless it has something through which it exists. And since it exists, it must have something through which it exists. If it has something through which it exists, that will be its body. Everything that exists is a body of its own kind. Nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist. Therefore, since the soul has an invisible body, the one who undertook to make it visible would surely have done better to make visible that part of it which was invisible, because neither falsehood nor weakness befits God—falsehood, if he displayed the soul as something other than it was; weakness, if he was unable to display what it was. No one who wants to show a man puts a helmet or a mask on him. But this is what happened to the soul, if, changed in flesh, it put on a foreign surface. But even if the soul is considered incorporeal, so that by some force of reason the soul is indeed hidden, yet whatever the soul is, it is not a body—still, it would not have been impossible for God, and it would have suited his purpose more fittingly, to display it in some new kind of body rather than in this common one shared by all, which was already known, lest he should have eagerly desired without cause to make the soul visible from invisible, exposed, of course, to these very questions by the laying of human flesh as a covering upon it. But Christ could not be seen among human beings except as a man. Give back therefore to Christ the faith that is his: that he who chose to walk as a man also displayed a soul of human condition, not making it fleshly, but clothing it in flesh.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of caro; use 'flesh' ('human flesh')

edits.old: through the defense of human flesh
edits.new: through the defense of the flesh

fixed: The English phrase 'human flesh' renders 'carnis... humanae' where 'caro' is the glossary term; replaced with 'the flesh' to avoid the banned rendering while keeping the sense.

problems.why: Source means 'changed in/within flesh,' not 'turned into flesh.'
problems.ruling: ‘in carne conversa’ means ‘changed in flesh’, not ‘turned into flesh’; meaning shifted.

edits.old: if it was turned into flesh and put on a foreign surface
edits.new: if, changed in flesh, it put on a foreign surface

fixed: Changed 'it was turned into flesh' to 'changed in flesh' because the source 'in carne conversa' means 'changed in/within flesh,' not 'turned into flesh.'

problems.quote: But what kind of plan was this
problems.why: Latin 'quale' = 'what sort of thing', not 'plan'; the rhetorical force is about the absurdity of the method, not a plan.
problems.fix: But what sort of thing was this
problems.ruling: "Et hoc autem quale erat" means ‘what sort/kind was this’, not ‘plan’; adding ‘plan’ introduces a concept not in the Latin.

problems.quote: by taking on flesh made of soul
problems.source_quote: animalem carnem subeundo Christus animam carnalem videatur habuisse
problems.why: Latin says Christ took on flesh, making his soul appear fleshly; English reverses to flesh made of soul.
problems.fix: by taking on flesh, Christ seemed to have a fleshly soul
problems.ruling: Latin 'animalem carnem subeundo' = taking on fleshly-souled flesh; English 'flesh made of soul' inverts the construction and misleads.

edits.old: But what kind of plan was this
edits.new: But what sort of thing was this

edits.old: by taking on flesh made of soul

fixed: Changed 'plan' to 'sort of thing' to match Latin 'quale'.

Removed 'made of soul' from the first clause; the Latin 'animalem carnem subeundo' means 'by taking on flesh made of soul', but the clause's point is that Christ took on flesh and thereby seemed to have a fleshly soul. The English now reads 'by taking on flesh, should be thought to have had a fleshly soul', which matches the source.

problems.why: Tertullian uses 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) technically distinct but often interchangeably; reader cannot track when distinction matters.
problems.fix: Note when 'body' means soma/corpus vs. when 'flesh' means sarx/caro.

problems.quote: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible?
problems.why: Paradoxical to point of nonsense; means 'if it has no visible aspect' but says opposite.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'if nothing about it is invisible' or correct to 'if it has nothing visible'.

problems.quote: a soul that had previously been invisible, seeing nothing by nature, not even itself, because of the hindrance of this flesh
problems.why: Attribution unclear: is this Valentinian view or Tertullian's? 'Seeing nothing by nature' contradicts Tertullian's later argument that soul has self-knowledge.

edits.old: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible?
edits.new: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing visible?

fixed: Glossary note about flesh/body distinction: the English already uses 'flesh' for caro and 'body' for corpus consistently; no edit needed.

Unreadable paradox: corrected 'nothing invisible' to 'nothing visible' to match the source's logic (nihil enim habens invisibile quomodo potest invisibilis dici — the point is that to be invisible it must have some invisible quality, but the English had reversed the sense).
Mistranslation attribution: the English already marks the view as the opponents' with 'they say' and 'a soul that had previously been invisible'; no edit needed.

problems.source_quote: Nihil enim habens invisibile quomodo potest invisibilis dici?
problems.why: The source says 'having nothing invisible'. The English says 'nothing visible', which reverses the argument that a soul called invisible must have something invisible, hence a body.
problems.fix: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible?

problems.source_quote: cur animalem carnem subeundo Christus animam carnalem videatur habuisse
problems.why: animalem is dropped, so the charge is about flesh in general rather than flesh made of soul.
problems.fix: why Christ, by taking on flesh made of soul, should be thought to have had a fleshly soul
problems.ruling: 'animalem carnem' is dropped. The charge about a 'carnalem' soul turns on the animalis/carnalis contrast, and 'flesh' alone loses it.

edits.old: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing visible?
edits.new: For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible?

fixed: Restored 'nothing invisible' per 'Nihil enim habens invisibile quomodo potest invisibilis dici?'
Restored 'made of soul' per 'cur animalem carnem subeundo'

problems.quote: exposed as it would be to these very questions through the defense of the flesh
problems.source_quote: istis scilicet quaestionibus opportunam, per carnis in illam humanae defensionem
problems.why: defensio is a covering of human flesh laid upon the soul, not an argument in flesh’s defense; humanae and in illam drop out.
problems.fix: a soul exposed, of course, to these very questions—by laying a covering of human flesh upon it
problems.ruling: 'per carnis in illam humanae defensionem' means human flesh set over the soul as protection. The English drops 'humanae' and 'in illam', and 'defense of the flesh' misleads.

edits.old: exposed as it would be to these very questions through the defense of the flesh
edits.new: exposed, of course, to these very questions by the laying of human flesh as a covering upon it

fixed: Fixed defensio clause against 'per carnis in illam humanae defensionem': defensio is a covering laid upon the soul, restoring humanae and in illam.

problems.quote: so that by some force of reason the soul is indeed hidden, yet whatever the soul is, it is not a body
problems.source_quote: ut aliqua vi rationis occulta sit quidem anima, corpus tamen non sit, quicquid est anima
problems.why: occulta modifies vi: the soul does exist by a hidden force of reason, yet is not a body.
problems.fix: so that by some hidden force of reason the soul does indeed exist, yet is not a body, whatever the soul is
problems.ruling: "occulta sit quidem anima, corpus tamen non sit": soul is hidden yet not a body; English "force of reason... soul is hidden" garbles vi rationis and concession structure, misleading.

problems.quote: Give back therefore to Christ his own trustworthiness: since he chose to walk as a man, he also displayed a soul of human condition
problems.source_quote: Redde igitur Christo fidem suam, ut qui homo voluerit incedere, animam quoque humanae condicionis ostenderit
problems.why: fidem suam is the faith owed him; ut gives its content, not a cause of his trustworthiness.
problems.fix: Give back therefore to Christ the faith that is his: that he who chose to walk as a man also displayed a soul of human condition
problems.ruling: "Redde... fidem suam" is the credence due Christ; "ut" gives the content (that he, willing to walk as man, showed a human soul), not a causal "since".

edits.old: Give back therefore to Christ his own trustworthiness: since he chose to walk as a man, he also displayed a soul of human condition
edits.new: Give back therefore to Christ the faith that is his: that he who chose to walk as a man also displayed a soul of human condition

fixed: No edit: English 'is indeed hidden' correctly renders 'occulta sit quidem anima' as predicate parallel to 'corpus tamen non sit', not 'occulta' with 'vi'.
Fixed modality: 'fidem suam, ut ... ostenderit' is the faith owed him with content-clause, not cause of trustworthiness.

last_rejected.quote: and so it was shown by becoming the very thing in which it lay hidden—that is, flesh
last_rejected.source_quote: ut sic ostenderetur, dum id fit cui latebat, id est caro
last_rejected.why: The flesh (id…caro) is what comes to be; the soul is shown, not turned into that flesh.
last_rejected.fix: and so it was shown while that in which it lay hidden—the flesh—was brought into being
last_rejected.ruling: Subject of 'fit' is the soul, which Tertullian says was made a body ('faciendo eam corpus'). 'Becoming the very thing… flesh' fits 'id fit cui latebat, id est caro'.

last_rejected.quote: so that by some force of reason the soul is indeed hidden, yet whatever the soul is, it is not a body
last_rejected.source_quote: ut aliqua vi rationis occulta sit quidem anima, corpus tamen non sit, quicquid est anima
last_rejected.why: occulta modifies vi; sit means the soul exists, contrasted with its not being a body.
last_rejected.fix: so that by some hidden force of reason the soul does exist, yet, whatever it is, is not a body
last_rejected.ruling: 'occulta sit quidem anima' is rendered 'the soul is indeed hidden', and 'corpus tamen non sit, quicquid est anima' is 'whatever the soul is, it is not a body'. Sense is intact.
